---
title: "Attackability"
---

How attackable each statement is *by a bounded automated proof campaign*: a machine-checked
estimate of whether pointing a multi-agent harness at it would produce a correct, non-vacuous,
novel result inside a fixed budget. Every statement under `c/` carries one, scored on a fixed
scale on 23 August 2026.

## This is not the difficulty grade, and not a ranking of truth

Two axes, easy to confuse, deliberately separate.

The [difficulty grade](/reviews/status-badge/index.qmd#difficulty-legend) each statement carries is
*distance from known technique*: what a resolution would have to invent. It says nothing about who
is working or with what.

Attackability is the other thing that legend disclaims -- expected effort for one specific worker
with specific compute. It is not a probability that the statement is true, not a probability it will
be resolved, and not a judgement of how interesting it is. **A statement can be easy for a human
expert and hard here, or the reverse.** [c/0001](/c/0001/) is the first case: the six-round Feistel
gap is one rung wide and a human knows exactly what to try, but the deliverable is a simulator, which
has no scalar score and no small-case decision procedure, so it scores 11. [c/0015](/c/0015/) is the
second: a combinatorial approximation ratio that no expert has bothered with, exhaustively decidable
at ten leaves, scoring 25.

Reading attackability as importance would get the corpus exactly backwards. Eight of the top nine
scores here sit on statements their own source raised in a sentence and never returned to, and six of
them carry no idealized model at all -- Fourier analysis on abelian groups, finite martingales, binary
trees, matrix recovery, reweightings on the sphere. They score high because a reading cannot drift, a
small case can be decided exactly, and there is nothing to compose. That is a statement about
tractability and about nobody having bothered, and about nothing else.

## The eight axes

Three groups, maximum 31. Each axis has a stated reason on the record; a score without one is
decoration.

**P, proof-path tractability (max 12).** `P1` directionality: is the machine-friendly side the side
being asked for? Construction search finds objects, not lower bounds. `P2` ladder quality: is there
an explicit restriction axis with a settled base case, and a next rung whose surviving mechanism can
be named? `P3` technique proximity: how many independent published results must be composed, and how
much unstated context from their preliminaries does the statement silently depend on. A route needing
a genuinely new framework caps `P3` at 1: long is fine, novel is not.

**V, verification tractability (max 12).** `V1` statement determinacy, weighted heaviest at 6,
because drift is the failure that survives verification -- a correct proof of the wrong statement
passes every local check. `V2` refutation affordance: is there a finite instantiation where the claim
is decidable by exact computation, and can the predicate be hardened against being gamed? `V3`
formalization reach: does a matching proof assistant exist, is the lemma decomposition cheap for a
human to write, and is there a machine-checkable witness short of a full proof.

**O, opportunity (max 7).** `O1` obscurity dividend: open status usually reflects obscurity rather
than difficulty, so a conjecture stated in one line and never returned to scores above a named
conjecture with a tradition. `O2` source access and campaign fit.

**Risk deductions.** Contamination (the answer may sit in training data, which inflates apparent
success and destroys the novelty claim), vacuity, ladder length, predicate exploitability, expert
scarcity.

## Bands

The band is the inverse reading of the same number. It is difficulty **for this harness**, and its
names are deliberately not the difficulty grades: nothing here is called `routine`, `adaptation`,
`new-idea` or `barrier`.

| Band | Score | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `prime` | 26 to 31 | Everything the scale rewards is present. Run it first. |
| `reachable` | 22 to 25 | A full campaign is worth resourcing. |
| `stretch` | 18 to 21 | Worth a scout, a refuter and a case planner, then re-triage. No prover wave. |
| `hard` | 15 to 17 | Same, and expect the cheap refutation to be the whole return. |
| `very hard` | 8 to 14 | Expect a barrier note, not a proof. |
| `out of reach` | 0 to 7 | Do not resource a proof attempt. |
| `gated` | n/a | Stopped before scoring. See below. |

Verdicts follow mechanically from the axes, never by hand: `go` at 22 or more with both `P` and `V`
clearing a floor of 7, `probe` from 15, `park` below. The floors are quality gates rather than a
reason to park a strong candidate, so a statement scoring 22 or more that misses one of them lands at
`probe`. Two overrides matter. A statement whose reading
cannot be pinned is capped at `probe` however high it scores, because a proof you cannot audit is not
evidence. And maximal cheap refutability promotes a `park` to a `probe`, because a counterexample is
cheap to check and expensive to overlook -- which is why [c/0050](/c/0050/), [c/0051](/c/0051/) and
[c/0053](/c/0053/) appear as probes despite scoring 11, 12 and 14.

## What the pass found

**Fourteen statements were gated before scoring.** A gate stops a campaign; it is not a low score.

Two hit a transferred barrier: a proof would resolve a named open problem elsewhere.
[c/0011](/c/0011/) is unconditional as stated, and its source records that an unconditional proof
would imply that one-way functions exist and that P is not NP. [c/0056](/c/0056/) is gated by its own
source's Theorem 4. In both cases the *refutation* direction is unobstructed and cheap, and that is
where any budget should go.

Five need their statement fixed before anything else. [c/0016](/c/0016/) asks for a class of query
distributions without naming it, so identifying the class is part of the problem rather than a
hypothesis of it; the repair is already written on its own page. [c/0040](/c/0040/) is stated against a
definition its page describes as departing from the source's in three ways, under a hardness
hypothesis the source offers only as an example. [c/0019](/c/0019/), [c/0039](/c/0039/) and
[c/0003](/c/0003/) turn on load-bearing definitions their sources never give.

**[c/0003](/c/0003/) is the one to fix first, because the statement as written is false.** The oracle
carries no salt, so the offline stage can store a single k-collision in k log N bits and the online
stage can output it with no queries at all, winning with probability tending to one while the claimed
tradeoff is violated outright. The whole literature the page cites is stated relative to a salt drawn
after the advice is fixed, and the k = 2 baseline in its own comparison table is a salted theorem
transcribed without its salt. Adding the salt makes it a real open problem again.

**Seven were already resolved.** Six confirm the site's own August sweep: [c/0018](/c/0018/),
[c/0026](/c/0026/), [c/0027](/c/0027/) (refuted, not proved), [c/0037](/c/0037/), [c/0038](/c/0038/),
[c/0046](/c/0046/). [c/0004](/c/0004/) is resolved in-repo by a proof that has not been reviewed, so
its remaining work is verification rather than proving.

**One state of the art was stale.** [c/0024](/c/0024/) carried a caveat saying its citing papers had
not been checked. They have been now: a CRYPTO 2024 follow-up reaches a hardness gap of `N^1.6` in
Maurer's model under exponentially hard injective pseudorandom generators. That does not settle the
page, whose statement is information-theoretic, but it adds a rung the page does not record, and it is
exactly the object a produced solution would be mistaken for.

**Four pairs can silently answer each other's question.** [c/0008](/c/0008/) and [c/0009](/c/0009/)
share a byte-identical LaTeX source stating two conjectures, and only the frontmatter says which page
is which; so do [c/0004](/c/0004/) and [c/0005](/c/0005/). [c/0050](/c/0050/) and [c/0053](/c/0053/)
differ by one word, quantum. [c/0024](/c/0024/) and [c/0025](/c/0025/) differ by which generic group
model. Any attempt on one of these has to name its sibling explicitly, or a correct proof of the
neighbour's statement will pass every check.

**The corpus is not lower-bound dominated,** which is the usual failure mode of an open-problem
archive: 27 statements ask for a construction against 20 asking for a lower bound. The clearest case
is a pair. [c/0051](/c/0051/), the sponge STB conjecture, scores 12 and survives only on cheap
refutability. [c/0052](/c/0052/), which asks for the attack that would refute it, is the same
mathematics from the machine-friendly side and scores 24. Where a statement is a lower bound, the
record carries its construction-side dual, and that dual is usually the thing worth attacking.

## What this is worth, honestly

Every grade here is machine-made, in one pass, by one model. The scale is anchored on four worked
examples and the totals, verdicts, overrides and bands are all derived from the axis scores rather
than asserted, so the arithmetic is checkable and the judgement is not. Three things are outstanding.
The scores were re-derived once in the same session rather than in a fresh one, and that re-derivation
moved four of them by a point each, which suggests a genuinely independent pass would move more.
Several records rest on a source read only through the site's own restatement rather than in full;
those are flagged per record. And the deductions for contamination are estimates, not measurements:
where a nearby result sits in training data, apparent success and real success are hard to tell apart
without re-checking the technique rather than the statement.

Grades round towards *harder than it looks*, on the same principle as the badge.

## Provenance

Produced by the `conjecture-triage` skill on 23 August 2026 over all 55 statements under `c/`.
[c/0005](/c/0005/) is excluded: it was withdrawn at its author's request and is no longer tracked as
an open problem. The remaining 54 records, with the full per-axis reasons, the scout evidence and its
retrieval tags, the construction-side duals and the entry rung proposed for each campaign, are in
[the audit record](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/audits/2026-08-23-conjecture-attackability-triage.md)
and its
[machine-readable companion](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/audits/2026-08-23-conjecture-attackability-triage.records.jsonl).
This page is a dated snapshot of those records, not a live view: attackability is not yet a statement
field, and deliberately so until the research-object data model lands.
